title: Dynamic Reasoning in Next-Gen Detection and Response: An Empirical Study of LLM Triage, Reinforcement Tuning, and Adversarial Evasion
authors: Jeremy Canale
abstract: We present an end-to-end empirical study of dynamic reasoning in next-generation detection and response pipelines, evaluating how static classifiers, graph-based signal fusion, and large language model (LLM) triage agents perform under strict human-analyst attention budgets (Recall at B alerts/day). title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
authors: Catarina Botelho, António Farinhas, John Mendonça et al.
abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
authors: Saket Reddy, Ke Yang, ChengXiang Zhai
abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
authors: Albert Chiwara, Erhan Guven
abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. title: The Geometry Is the Memory: Task-Density Routing for Continual LoRA
authors: Alireza Heidari, Thomas Veasey, Mariano Tepper
abstract: Freezing older adapters does not ensure that a continual learner will select and use them properly at inference time. When multiple adapters exist, routing among them and identifying the adapter whose representation space matches the query's answer can be difficult. title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
authors: Kaidi Fu, Xu-Hao Lu, Pingwei Sun et al.
abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. title: Joint Estimation of Abilities and Item Parameters for Large Language Models Using Probability and Binary Responses: A Fractional-Response IRT Framework
authors: Masayuki Takayama, Shohei Shimizu
abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations provide two response types: probabilities assigned to correct answers and binary indicators of correctness. Restricting evaluation to one type narrows the range of available models or discards probability information. We propose a method to integrate both types through a common two-parameter logistic item response model and fractional-response quasi-maximum likelihood estimation. title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
authors: Luiz G. A. Alves, Aaron Vermeersch
abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
authors: Yage Zhang, Yukun Jiang, Ziqing Yang et al.
abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. authors: Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen
abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? title: Collaborative Language Models for Semantic IoT Data Processing: Validation through Zero-Shot Human Activity Recognition
authors: Mohsen Shirali, Kean Ooi, Anna Knab et al.
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems generate low-level sensor observations that are not directly suitable for process analysis and must first be transformed into semantically meaningful events. This paper investigates collaborative language models as a zero-shot semantic abstraction layer for converting such observations into higher-level event and activity labels. title: RoboARC: Physical Puzzles for Robotic Manipulation under Spatial Constraints
authors: Qineng Wang, Jianwen Lyu, Pingyue Zhang et al.
abstract: Many hard manipulation tasks come down to a spatial constraint that only a few motions satisfy, such as passing a part through a gap barely wider than itself or separating two interlocked parts. These motions depend on the exact geometry of each scene, so demonstrations and skills recorded elsewhere rarely transfer. title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
authors: Microsoft CodeAI Team,  Microsoft VS Code Team, Julia Gong et al.
abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
authors: Wenlong Yu, Bingxu Lu, Qilong Wang et al.
abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Mathijs A. Langezaal, Egon L. van den Broek, Lukas P. A. Arts et al.
abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance
authors: Hansi Zhang+, Wilma Johanna Schmidt+, Wanlin Yang et al.
abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. title: Automated Call for Action: RAG-Based Environmental Law Enforcement Screening System
authors: Matas Jurkevicius, Yen-Chia Hsu
abstract: Environmental law inspectors face a structural issue in identifying potential violations from data: they often do not have the capacity to deal with large volume of data present in the emission events. This paper examines to what extent an LLM-based system can support evidence assembly and permit-based screening of such events, using the coke plants of a steel producer and a regional environmental service as a case. title: MH-RAG-DIVE: Dynamic and Cost-Efficient Multi-Hop RAG Evaluation via Tree-Cached Dialogue Simulation
authors: Lorenz Brehme, Daniel Hillebrand, Thomas Ströhle et al.
abstract: Quality assessment is essential for determining whether changes to a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system improve or maintain its performance. However, existing evaluation approaches often rely on single-turn or single-hop interactions and therefore do not capture the complexity of multi-hop, multi-turn conversations. title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Agentic Era: Tradition, Present, and Prospect
authors: Chenming Tang, Haolin Li, Yiran Li et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) couples frozen language models with external, updatable knowledge, so that generation is grounded in retrieved evidence rather than in parametric memory alone. This work maps RAG in the agentic era by joining them on a single lifecycle axis, from offline indexing through pre-retrieval, retrieval, post-retrieval, and orchestration over these stages. title: SHAKTI: Evidence-Grounded Conversational AI for Nutrition and Health
authors: Chaitanya Pallerla, Dongyi Wang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) answer many diet and health questions but can state unsupported claims and cite sources that do not support them. We present SHAKTI (Smart Health Advisor for Knowledge-based Tailored Interventions), a conversational assistant that answers only from retrieved scholarly papers and exact food-composition data, and evaluate it with retrieval, generation, grounding, efficiency and contextawareness metrics. title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
authors: Ramraj Chandradevan, Sayontan Ghosh, Vinoth Selvendran
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
authors: Tianyi Huang, Samuel Xu, Ivy Gu et al.
abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
authors: Tianrun Gou, Qingyao Yang, Wendong Xu et al.
abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments
authors: Yulliwas Ameur, Miqeas Pedro Mendes, Samia Bouzefrane
abstract: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. title: Transport-Safe Evaluation of LLM Agents: Trajectory-Dependent Judge Error and Anytime-Valid Auditing
authors: Yulliwas Ameur, Samia Bouzefrane, Soumya Banerjee
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often ranked by an LLM judge whose error rates are measured once and reused for every agent. The corrected success rates can then be biased when the judge's errors depend on the trajectory and agents differ in the trajectories they produce for successes or failures. title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
authors: Igor Santos-Grueiro, Daniel Romero-Ruiz
abstract: LLM agents act through tool calls: the model writes the arguments of a call as JSON, a guard decides whether the call may run, and an executor runs it. The same bytes are parsed several times, by the provider, gateways, SDKs, frameworks, the guard, and the executor. JSON leaves some choices to each parser, such as which copy of a repeated key counts. title: HWRE-Bench: Can LLM Agents Understand Hardware They Did Not Design?
authors: Peilong Zhou, Cangyuan Li, Kaiyan Chang et al.
abstract: Hardware benchmarks for LLM agents all run the design flow forward, from a specification to RTL, a layout or a bug fix. We ask the reverse question: given an implemented artifact, such as a layout, a gate-level netlist or a protected simulation model, can an agent work out what it does well enough to act on that knowledge? title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments
authors: Yi-Fei Cao, Tianxin Huang, Hanbo Xie et al.
abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. title: RepoClean: Evaluating Coding Agents on Repository-Level Obsolete Code Cleanup
authors: Hongyixuan Yuan, Qixing Zhou, Pengcheng Huang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong repository-level programming capabilities. However, as software evolves, repository code may become redundant or obsolete, increasing maintenance costs and potentially introducing functional issues. Agents must therefore identify and remove unnecessary code safely, yet autonomous repository-level code cleanup remains insufficiently evaluated in isolation. title: Attributing Security Outcomes in LLM-Agent Evaluations: The Role of Content-Free State
authors: Abdelmonaim Bounite, Zangir Iklassov
abstract: Security benchmarks for LLM agents record whether each attack succeeded and compare agents, attacks, and defenses by attack success rate (ASR). Such comparisons are valid only if the agent, the attack, and the defense cause each verdict. title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
authors: Xinran Zhao, Xiang Li, Tong Chen et al.
abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents
authors: Zirui Zhu, Cong Zhang, Ni Zhang et al.
abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. title: GlobalHRBench: Does Changing the Question Language Change the Legal Answer?
authors: Yuding Wang, Yuhang Yao
abstract: Language matters when deploying LLM agents across borders, especially in law, where the governing rules must hold across working languages. Does changing the language of a legal question change answer accuracy? We introduce GlobalHRBench, pairing 240 employment-law problems across eight jurisdictions and eight languages while fixing facts, applicable law and required conclusions. title: Can Latent Reasoning Drive LLM Outputs Without a Trace?
authors: Tomer Ashuach, Zorik Gekhman, Avi Caciularu et al.
abstract: LLMs typically solve complex tasks with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, which is also the main tool for monitoring them for misaligned behavior. However, standard transformers can also solve tasks with complete latent reasoning (CLR), carrying out the whole task internally and outputting only the final answer. title: Beyond Self-Consistency: Recursive Self-Improvement at Test Time
authors: Jianyu Wu, Yizhou Wang, Encheng Su et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) that continue improving after deployment (e.g., recursive self-improvement) offer a promising path toward general intelligence. Current test-time methods pursue this goal on unlabeled questions, primarily relying on self-consistency: they generate independent solutions and use majority voting to select an answer or construct training targets. title: Semantic-aware Decoding for Diverse Text-to-SQL under Schema Ambiguity
authors: Yuxuan Jiang, Anna Mitsopoulou, Apostolos Koukouvinis et al.
abstract: Real-world text-to-SQL systems often face schema ambiguity, where a question can map to multiple plausible schema elements. To support downstream disambiguation, SQL generation systems should include diverse interpretations among their top-k predictions. However, large language models (LLMs) typically favor a single interpretation, producing highly skewed outputs. title: From Rewarding What Models Say to How They Think: Attention Process Reward Model for LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kairong Han, Nuanqiao Shan, Ziyu Zhao et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component in large language models (LLMs). However, existing RL approaches focus on final outputs or textual solution trajectories, leading to coarse-grained rewards and unreliable reasoning. Such paradigms focus mainly on what the model outputs while overlooking how the model internally reasons. Therefore, can we reward how a model thinks internally rather than merely what it says? title: Auxiliary Clues Aware's Geometry Problem Solving
authors: Qigong Lei, Qingsong Wang, Wang Lin et al.
abstract: Geometry Problem Solving (GPS) serves as a rigorous test of the complex reasoning capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), particularly when solutions require auxiliary constructions absent from the input diagram. title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
authors: Junrui Zhang, Zeyu Xu, Runchuan Zhu et al.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. title: Test-Time Latent Computation to Improve Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Chen Yang, Zheng Fang, Wenqi Fan et al.
abstract: Recent work on Large Language Models (LLMs) suggests that reasoning capabilities can be enhanced at test time not only through longer token-level reasoning traces, but also through additional computation in latent space. This raises a natural question for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs): can additional computation in latent space improve visual perception at test time? title: Learning Heterogeneous Reasoning in Large Language Models: From Mode Compatibility to Local Bottlenecks
authors: Sunbowen Li, Dandan Song, Shengkun Ma et al.
abstract: Post-training large language models routinely pools reasoning trajectories from diverse teachers or algorithms, yet it remains unclear whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can learn such heterogeneous strategies without explicit mode conditioning. authors: Yusong Zhao, Zihao Zhao, Zirui Zhang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. title: Semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash on H5N1 One Health questions
authors: Luizza Dalla Pria, Amelia l. Nelson, Renata Ivanek
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
authors: Rui Sun, Junhua Huang, Luca Zancato et al.
abstract: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. title: Parsing Visual Latents for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
authors: Zhuoying Yang, Yichen Guo, Kathy Jia et al.
abstract: Spatial reasoning across multiple views requires inferring the 3D relations between objects and the camera from 2D observations, which depends on cross-view correspondence and scene geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) do not reliably extract. title: Replay Before You Reply: Second-Look Prompting for Unified Multimodal Encoding
authors: Yicheng Zhang, Xun Zhang, Jingyuan Ma et al.
abstract: Solving multimodal tasks requires Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to form a unified understanding of the image and the question text. However, under causal attention in current VLMs, a token can attend only to what precedes it. Whichever modality comes first is therefore encoded under partial observation of the input, uninformed by the rest of the multimodal context. title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce
authors: Binhui Xie, Jinmin Li, Haomiao Tang et al.
abstract: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Contrastive Decoding for Hallucination Mitigation in Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Ting Chen, Geng Li, Guohao Chen et al.
abstract: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. title: TamperCert: A Benchmark for Detecting Text Tampering in Degree Certificates
authors: ChiFung Kwan, Kangzhong Wang, Youqian Zhang et al.
abstract: Degree certificates play a critical role in high-stakes decisions such as university admission, immigration, and hiring. The issuing institution vouches for the holder, so a forged certificate may let its bearer pass these checks. Degree certificate forgery is increasingly prevalent. Yet, many assume that it is easy to spot. authors: Yuxuan Chen, Changwei Lv, Yunfei Li et al.
abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. title: Uncovering Hidden Behaviours in Language Models via Limited-Parameter Finetuning
authors: Boyd Kane, Jo J. Jiao, Elizabeth Donoway et al.
abstract: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore limited-parameter finetuning (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. title: WASP: Continual Weight Adaptation for Streaming LLM Personalization
authors: Linxi Xie, Chonghua Liao, Mengxuan Wu et al.
abstract: Personalized large language models (LLMs) should continually adapt to users' evolving preferences. Yet extracting preference changes from noisy interaction histories while supporting inexpensive updates remains challenging. We introduce WASP (Weight Adaptation for Streaming Personalization), a recurrent framework that captures fine-grained preferences directly from raw user interactions and generates personalized LoRA adapters without expensive per-user optimization. title: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Melika Shirian, Kianoosh Vadaei, Arshia Hemmat et al.
abstract: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. authors: Peter Horvath, Ilia Shumailov, Zhuoran Liu et al.
abstract: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. authors: Vladislav Mikhailov, Sarfraz Ahmad, Momina Ahsan et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects
authors: Ruichen Qiu, Hao Shen, Lihong Zhi et al.
abstract: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned r

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one cli

title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation
authors: Wenyang Gao, Yinghao Yang, Xi Jin et al.
abstract: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across t

title: Could This BE Any More Wrong? Teaching VLMs to Know What They Don't Know in Document Extraction
authors: Varad Srivastava, Victor Casas Hernandez
abstract: Vision-Language Models can extract structured fields from scanned financial documents, yet they provide no indication of when a field might be wrong. We derive per-field confidence estimates from the token log-probabilities the model already produces, via a token-to-span alignment procedure that maps logprobs onto each extracted value within the structured JSON output. title: How Relations Impose Embedding-Space Structure
authors: Lachlan Cowley, Jey Han Lau, Yulia Otmakhova et al.
abstract: Language models are known to encode simple relations, such as synonymy, in the geometry of their representations. It is unclear whether they also encode complex patterns of relationships such as those that drive analogy. We present a simple method, with no learned parameters, based on comparing the internal structural arrangements between disparate domains, to test this. Using our method we find over multiple models that representations are arranged consistently to encode complex relationship si

title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
authors: Nan Chen, Soledad Villar, Soufiane Hayou
abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
authors: Yanzhe Chen, Zhijun Cao, Zechen Bai et al.
abstract: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
authors: Zhengyang Wang, Renfei Tan, Shuze Daniel Liu et al.
abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for

title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture
authors: Xulong Wang, Yu Zhang, Gaoshan Bi et al.
abstract: In agriculture, typically over half of the applied nitrogen fertiliser is lost to water and to air. Precision fertilisation aims to reduce these losses while maintaining yield and quality, yet existing tools struggle to capture farm-specific challenges in determining optimal nitrogen rates. Static recommendations are common and overlook on-farm constraints, such as delays due to weather or machinery availability, or change in budgets. Each constraint governs when and how growers apply fertiliser

title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
authors: Marvin Kopka, Austen El-Osta, Christoph Kollwitz et al.
abstract: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synt

title: RoboUniverse-10K: Toward the Scaling Era of Agentic Robotics via Real-to-Sim Environments
authors: Jinkun Liu, Yingze Wang, Situ Wang et al.
abstract: Agentic Robotics, in which foundation models act as coding agents to control robots through executable programs, has emerged as a compelling paradigm for embodied intelligence. Yet unlike software engineering, where massive executable environments power post-training, robotics remains constrained by small, manual benchmarks and in-distribution evaluation. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboUniverse-10K, 10,807 interactive, resettable, and verifiable physics environments built from real-world v

title: SARA: An Auditor-in-the-Loop LLM Recommender for Sustainability Reports
authors: Lars Hillebrand, Thiago B. F. de Oliveira, Tim Dilmaghani et al.
abstract: Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy, repeatedly revised draft reports and to judge compliance. We present SARA (Sustainability Reporting Assistant), a human-in-the-loop recommender system delivered as a Microsoft Word add-in that recommends, for each requirement, the passages addressing it and predicts a compliance verdict while keeping

title: What Quality Engineers Need to Know About Generative AI: Structured Data Extraction
authors: Fadel M. Megahed, Ying-Ju Chen, Yamin Dahwich et al.
abstract: In this expository paper, we explain how quality engineers can use large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for structured data extraction. We introduce the relevant concepts, discuss structured extraction from a measurement-system perspective, and demonstrate its implementation in R and Python. title: Trallie: from Free-Form Text to Structured Data with LLMs
authors: Vijayasri Iyer, Cristiano De Nobili, Mubashir Hussain Shah et al.
abstract: Trallie is an open-source framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to perform information extraction (IE) from natural language sources with or without user guidance. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets or domain-specific training, Trallie enables the conversion of unstructured data into structured formats with minimal or no representative examples. title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
authors: Yan Tan, Xiangchen Meng, Yangdi Lyu
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semant

title: How Many Parameters Does Forecasting Need? A Survey and Code-Level Audit of Lightweight Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
authors: Issam Ait Yahia, Abdelkader El Mahdaouy, Ismail Berrada
abstract: Long-term time series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, weather and finance, where forecasts are produced continuously and often on constrained hardware. Recent work has moved in two directions. One scales Transformers and pre-trained foundation models to millions or hundreds of millions of parameters. The other shows that models with only hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters remain competitive on the standard benchmarks. Existing surveys organize forecasting model

title: Uncovering the Tells: Efficient Black-Box Audits for LLM Data Contamination
authors: Dominik Bernard Lau, Filip Pawlicki, Jan Dubiński et al.
abstract: Existing methods for assessing training data contamination in Large Language Models achieve high accuracy, but fundamentally rely on gray-box access, rendering them inapplicable to fully black-box environments. This limitation forces auditors to rely on full-sequence sampling or rigid heuristics, both of which incur prohibitive inference costs and struggle to isolate the underlying memorization signal. title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
authors: Merel Kuijs, Till Richter, Rushin H. Gindra et al.
abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder w

title: Quantizing Diffusion LLMs under Parallel Decoding: Commitment Risk and the Parallelism Tax
authors: Huan Xu, Maosen Zhao, Pengtao Chen et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are served with accelerated decoders that cache context and commit, in one step, every masked position whose confidence clears a threshold. Yet post-training quantization of dLLMs has so far been calibrated and evaluated under fixed-step samplers without caching. title: HEART: Hierarchical Expert Adaptive Refinement Transformer for ECG Representation Learning
authors: Junho Song, Jong-Hwan Jang, Joon-Myoung Kwon et al.
abstract: Learning robust representations from electrocardiograms (ECGs) is challenging because repeated cardiac cycles coexist with subtle and sparse diagnostic cues in local morphology and rhythm-level context. Existing ECG foundation models commonly rely on Transformerbased patch encoders with uniformly shared dense refinement pathways, limiting adaptive processing across heterogeneous ECG tokens. title: PCC: Pivotal Channel Compensation for Layer Pruning of Large Language Models
authors: Xiangqian Wang, Yucheng Zhang, Zhaohong Jia et al.
abstract: Treating independent layers as the minimal pruning unit allows layer pruning to efficiently eliminate many redundant parameters and achieve high compression rates. Layer pruning has become a promising and prevalent structured pruning technique for large language models (LLMs). However, multi-layer removal can lead to significant performance degradation for LLMs. Although some works have explored various compensation methods for pruned layers, they are inefficient and costly. Observing that the e

title: Trustworthy agentic lunar robotics: safety-constrained contingent planning with a foundation-model planner
authors: Bingqi Huang, Bingchuan Wei, Yingkai Cai et al.
abstract: Sustained lunar-base operations require robots that restore equipment and deliver cargo under conditions unforeseen before deployment. Flown space autonomy executes pre-validated procedures and enters a safe hold outside their scope, whereas foundation models synthesize plans on site that cannot be verified before execution. title: Audio-Visual Rearrangement
authors: Ruohao Guo, Jiatong Ye, Chenwei Dong et al.
abstract: We introduce Audio-Visual Rearrangement (AVR), a novel task in which an agent hears a spoken request, retrieves a suitable object, and delivers it to the requesting user or an instruction-specified destination. AVR requires the agent to understand the spoken request and acoustically localize the speaker for delivery. title: Parameter-Efficient Vocabulary Expansion via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment
authors: Andrew Ivan Soegeng, Muhammad Reza Qorib, Weishi Wang et al.
abstract: Continual pretraining with vocabulary expansion is often used to make large language models (LLMs) more effective and efficient at handling new languages. However, when LLMs are extended to many languages simultaneously, the number of model parameters increases significantly. In addition, the newly added tokens do not receive the same number of training steps as the tokens in the original vocabulary, which sometimes causes vocabulary expansion to yield only limited performance improvements. title: Character Information in Language Models: A Prompt-Independent Word Store and a Late, Question-Driven Signal That Grows With Scale
authors: Pratyush Acharya, Nuraj Rimal, Apar Baral et al.
abstract: Linear probes recover character properties of a word from a language model's hidden states, but a probe at the answer position cannot say whether the property was stored with the word or produced because the prompt asked for it. We separate the two with a word-position baseline: the same held-out-word probe applied to the query word's own tokens in a sentence that asks nothing. title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning
authors: Sushant Mehta, Logan Ritchie, Edwin Chen
abstract: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. title: LLM-Assisted Software Migration: from Module-Level Transformation to Repository-Level Integration
authors: Yanan Zhang, Shengqi Liu, Tao Zhang et al.
abstract: Software migration adapts an existing implementation to a new language, version, API, framework, or platform while preserving its behavior. Large language models (LLMs) succeed on individual functions and modules, but this success does not readily carry over to entire repositories, particularly deployable applications. This survey reviews LLM-assisted migration from module-level transformation to repository-level integration, culminating in the delivery of complete applications. We analyze 96 so

title: Training-Free Interventions for Hallucination in Large Language Models
authors: Can Huang
abstract: A frozen language model can give a wrong answer because a fact is unavailable, a reliable passage is ignored, or an unsupported claim survives generation. We review 116 works on inference-time hallucination intervention and its foundations. We trace the development from retrieval and controllable generation to methods that act on input evidence, token scores, internal representations, completed claims, or the decision to answer. For each family we compare its source of evidence, model access, pr

title: Landscape and Taxonomy of Prompt Engineering Patterns in Software Engineering
authors: Yuya Sasaki, Hironori Washizaki, Jialong Li et al.
abstract: Advancements in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced their ability to handle ambiguous user instructions. However, effective prompt patterns remain crucial for usability and comprehension. This article presents a taxonomy of prompt engineering patterns for software engineering. It is based on a systematic literature review that was conducted in early 2023, when LLMs still faced significant limitations in context length and inference capabilities. Our study explores techniques that enhance

title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
authors: Nicolas Bolouri, Gaya Mehenni, Daniel Toyama
abstract: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluat

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
authors: Yitong Qiao, Lei Liu, Yue Shen et al.
abstract: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states fr

title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero
authors: Yihao Shen, Yuxuan Chen, Xuantong Liu et al.
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
authors: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. title: Evaluating Persona Consistency in LLM User Simulators Without External Reference Annotations
authors: Anping Zhang, Yang Tan, Yipeng Liu et al.
abstract: Standard evaluations assess LLM-simulated personas against an external ground truth, such as community trait annotations, but that reference is unavailable when the persona is inferred only from a short, task-oriented chat. We ask how persona consistency can be evaluated without such a reference, and propose a self-anchored internal-consistency diagnostic: the persona describes itself once and acts twice. title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
authors: Keuntae Kim, Beomseok Lee, Hyunwoo Kim et al.
abstract: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. title: STMemoLLM: A Spatial-Temporal Memory-Augmented LLM for Robust Traffic Forecasting
authors: Jian Zhou, Binqing Wu, Zongjiang Shang et al.
abstract: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to comp

title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
authors: Chris Tava
abstract: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender

title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
authors: Javier Movellan, Manjot Bilkhu, Young-mok Jung et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time.

title: Multi-agent System for Automatic Discovery of Pareto-optimal Meta-solvers for PDEs
authors: Youngkyu Lee, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon et al.
abstract: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations requires problem-specific expertise. We present a multi-agent framework, in which language-model agents propose, critique, implement, and evaluate solver configurations assembled from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations, and neural operators. title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls
authors: Artem Trofimov, Boris Novikov
abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. title: Reproducible Social Structure Emerges From Free-Form Interaction Among LLM Agents
authors: Tom Alisch, Sonia Murthy, Robert Hawkins et al.
abstract: Multi-agent LLM simulations are increasingly used as models of social systems, but most published findings are anecdotal, i.e., drawn from a single run. It is therefore unclear which observed phenomena are robust findings of the simulated system itself, and which were random events in one particular run. title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
authors: Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Xuhui Li et al.
abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
authors: Chaeeun Lee, Hossein A. Rahmani, Aryo Pradipta Gema et al.
abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
authors: Gautam Choudhary, Jack Peng, Udesh Kumarasinghe et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
authors: Davood Wadi, Yu Ma
abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias.
